title: New software tool Pixasonics turns biomedical images into sound
excerpt: Modern biomedicine increasingly relies on enormous amounts of image data. Although computers can do part of the analysis work, biologists often still need to look through the images themselves. This takes time.
content_html:
Modern biomedicine increasingly relies on enormous amounts of image data. Although computers can do part of the analysis work, biologists often still need to look through the images themselves. This takes time.

"Therefore, we asked ourselves whether we could turn images into sound—so-called image sonification. This could prove useful in detecting patterns that are difficult to see with the naked eye," Bálint Laczkó says.

In close collaboration with colleagues at the University of Oslo, he has developed Pixasonics, a tool that can turn image data into sound. Its underlying method is freely available on GitHub. The software was presented last year at the 30th International Conference on Auditory Display (ICAD 2025). Laczkó will defend his dissertation on August 19 at the University of Oslo.

Published as a Python library

Today, various kinds of biological and medical research use image sonification, for instance in efforts to improve diagnosis. While some of the existing tools are research-oriented, others are mobile apps where you can upload an image and receive an audio representation in return.

Pixasonics uses the programming language Python and was created in collaboration with biologists in the project Autorhythm. The primary intended users are researchers in the life sciences, who can integrate it into programs they already use. Beyond that, it can be useful to other researchers, sound designers and musicians, according to Laczkó.

"It is a toolbox published as an open Python library. This means that it is a set of ready-made building blocks: When you write Python code, you can plug these blocks in so that you do not have to build everything yourself," he says.

However, if you wish to create something more unique, you can easily customize the blocks or build your own. "In this way, image sonification can be seamlessly integrated into your personal workflow."

Working to understand cells' recycling system

In the Autorhythm project, researchers are working toward a better understanding of the cells' own recycling system, called autophagy: The cells degrade and recycle protein clumps and structures that no longer function properly.

The older humans get, the more these processes weaken. This leads to a gradual destruction of the brain and other organs.

Research has indicated that strengthening the processes can be life-extending and that it may also open possibilities for better treatment of diseases—especially diseases in which nerve cells gradually deteriorate, such as Alzheimer's and Parkinson's. For this to happen, however, researchers must fully understand the autophagy process.

This is where Pixasonics comes in, since the work involves analysis of thousands of detailed images: Cell components are colored with so-called fluorescent proteins, which emit light, before biologists take a long series of high-resolution images, so-called time-lapses. In this way, they see what happens in the cells over time.

Sound reveals changes in an image series

"This is painstaking work, which can both give you sore eyes and involve a risk that important details are not detected," Laczkó explains.

With Pixasonics, biologists can upload the images they want to analyze and assign a specific task to the tool. The pixels in the image translate into sound, which plays in real time while the images are displayed on the screen.

"For example, a bright pixel can give a high, beeping tone and a dark pixel can give a deeper, rumbling tone. If you move the mouse pointer around, bright areas will make the pitch rise, while dark areas will make it fall."

Using the tool on an image series, you can hear how the subject changes over time. In this way, researchers will not have to jump back and forth between images to see what is happening in a particular area. The sound reveals how the image changes.

Can help find the needle in the haystack

"Our vision and hearing have evolved with different strengths. While vision is best at detecting spatial patterns, such as shapes, distance and position, hearing is best at perceiving patterns that unfold over time, for example rhythms, changes and sequences. Thus, a combination of eyes and ears can make large volumes of images easier to explore," Laczkó says.

Researchers, musicians and technologists have all contributed input to Pixasonics. Now he hopes to continue developing the tool, continue holding workshops and even conduct formal user studies.

"In addition, my colleagues and I have several ideas about how Pixasonics can become particularly useful in researching the cells' cleaning processes. For example, we believe that it can help find the needle in the haystack in cases where a tiny but important part of the autophagy process is buried in the sea of cells that are visible under the microscope," Laczkó says.

content_html_zh:
现代生物医学越来越依赖大量的图像数据。 尽管计算机可以完成部分分析工作，但生物学家通常仍然需要自己查看图像。 这需要时间。

“因此，我们问自己是否可以将图像转化为声音，即所谓的图像可听化。 这可能有助于检测肉眼难以看到的模式，”Bálint Laczkó 说。

他与奥斯陆大学的同事密切合作，开发了 Pixasonics，这是一种可以将图像数据转换为声音的工具。 其底层方法可以在 GitHub 上免费获得。 该软件于去年在第 30 届国际听觉显示会议 (ICAD 2025) 上发布。 Laczkó 将于 8 月 19 日在奥斯陆大学进行论文答辩。

发布为 Python 库

如今，各种生物和医学研究都使用图像超声处理，例如努力改善诊断。 虽然现有的一些工具是面向研究的，但其他工具是移动应用程序，您可以在其中上传图像并接收音频表示作为回报。

Pixasonics 使用 Python 编程语言，是与生物学家在 Autorhythm 项目中合作创建的。 主要的目标用户是生命科学研究人员，他们可以将其集成到他们已经使用的程序中。 拉茨科表示，除此之外，它对其他研究人员、声音设计师和音乐家也很有用。

“它是一个作为开放 Python 库发布的工具箱。 这意味着它是一组现成的构建块：当您编写 Python 代码时，您可以插入这些块，这样您就不必自己构建所有内容，”他说。

但是，如果您希望创建更独特的东西，您可以轻松自定义块或构建自己的块。 “通过这种方式，图像超声处理可以无缝集成到您的个人工作流程中。”

致力于了解细胞的回收系统

在 Autorhythm 项目中，研究人员正在努力更好地了解细胞自身的回收系统，即自噬：细胞降解并回收不再正常运作的蛋白质团块和结构。

人类年龄越大，这些过程就越弱。 这会导致大脑和其他器官逐渐遭到破坏。

研究表明，加强这些过程可以延长寿命，并且还可能为更好地治疗疾病提供可能性，尤其是神经细胞逐渐退化的疾病，例如阿尔茨海默氏症和帕金森氏症。 然而，要实现这一点，研究人员必须充分了解自噬过程。

这就是 Pixasonics 的用武之地，因为这项工作涉及对数千张详细图像的分析：在生物学家拍摄一长串高分辨率图像（即所谓的延时图像）之前，细胞成分会被所谓的荧光蛋白着色，这些荧光蛋白会发光。 通过这种方式，他们可以看到细胞随着时间的推移发生了什么。

声音揭示图像系列的变化

“这是一项艰苦的工作，不仅会让您眼睛酸痛，而且还存在无法检测到重要细节的风险，”Laczkó 解释道。

借助 Pixasonics，生物学家可以上传他们想要分析的图像，并向该工具分配特定任务。 图像中的像素转化为声音，声音在图像显示在屏幕上时实时播放。

“例如，明亮的像素可以发出高亢的蜂鸣声，而黑暗的像素可以发出更深沉的隆隆声。 如果你移动鼠标指针，明亮的区域会使音调上升，而黑暗的区域会使音调下降。”

在图像系列上使用该工具，您可以听到主题如何随时间变化。 这样，研究人员就不必在图像之间来回跳转来查看特定区域正在发生的情况。 声音揭示了图像如何变化。

可以帮助大海捞针

“我们的视觉和听觉已经进化出不同的优势。 视觉最擅长检测空间模式，例如形状、距离和位置，而听觉最擅长感知随着时间推移而展开的模式，例如节奏、变化和顺序。 因此，眼睛和耳朵的结合可以使大量图像更容易探索，”Laczkó 说。

研究人员、音乐家和技术专家都为 Pixasonics 做出了贡献。 现在他希望继续开发该工具，继续举办研讨会，甚至进行正式的用户研究。

“此外，我和我的同事对于 Pixasonics 如何在研究细胞清洁过程中变得特别有用有几个想法。 例如，我们相信，当自噬过程的一个微小但重要的部分被埋在显微镜下可见的细胞海洋中时，它可以帮助大海捞针，”Laczkó 说。
